meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You may not realize it when it happens, but a kick in the teeth may be the best thing in the world for you'?
meta.ogDescription: Real, and sourceable: page 89 of The Story of Walt Disney (1957), written by his daughter. The 1956 magazine version said 'kick in the pants' instead.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1901–1966 · American animator, film producer & studio founder
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The exact wording sits at page 89 of The Story of Walt Disney (Henry Holt and Company, New York, 1957) — the memoir Disney’s daughter Diane Disney Miller told to Saturday Evening Post writer Pete Martin, who wrote it up — where it is set inside quotation marks as Disney’s own words. A close variant reading “a kick in the pants” had already run in the Post on 1 December 1956, and Quote Investigator suspects Disney approved both formulations for publication.

source.excerpt: “I function better when things are going badly than when they’re as smooth as whipped cream,” he said. “When I’m in a fight I don’t worry, but when things are going good I’m afraid that something’s going to crack under me any minute. You may not realize it when it happens, but a kick in the teeth may be the best thing in the world for you.”
trail: 1 December 1956 — the earliest instance located by Quote Investigator ↗: “The Coming of the Mouse,” part of the Saturday Evening Post series “My Dad, Walt Disney” by Diane Disney Miller and Pete Martin, page 67 — carrying the “kick in the pants” wording.

1957 — the magazine material is revised into The Story of Walt Disney (Holt, New York, 247 pages), where page 89 carries the “kick in the teeth” form as Disney’s direct speech. The edition is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗.

1964–1969 — the “teeth” version spreads through compilations and newspaper filler: Alfred Armand Montapert’s Distilled Wisdom (Prentice-Hall, 1964, page 106), the Newark Advocate of 28 June 1966, and the Omaha World Herald of 10 July 1969, all logged by Quote Investigator ↗.
Today — Wikiquote ↗ carries it in its sourced Quotations section, cited to the 1957 book, and not among the Disney lines it flags as misattributed.
source.excerptNote: Page 89 as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from the 1957 book; the “he said” interjection is the book’s. The remark closes a longer passage in which Disney describes working better under difficulty, and the one-line form that circulates online is its tail. Separately, Wikiquote ↗ renders the line with a different lead-in — “All the adversity I’ve had in my life, all my troubles and obstacles, have strengthened me…” — citing the same 1957 book but giving no page.

source.rightsNote: The Story of Walt Disney was first published in 1957 — a US work from the 1929–1963 window, which remains in copyright if the registration was renewed in its 28th year. We have not found a renewal record either way, so treat the book as protected, and Disney’s remark as protected within that text rather than as a separately free-standing utterance. The earlier Saturday Evening Post printing of December 1956 falls in the same window and should likewise not be assumed free; quote it as an excerpt with attribution, not as public-domain material.

author.name: Walt Disney
author.heading: The man who said it
author.bio: Walt Disney (born 5 December 1901, died 15 December 1966) was an American animator, film producer, voice actor and entrepreneur who built the studio that bears his name. His career began with failure rather than fanfare: the Laugh-O-Gram company he founded in Kansas City went into bankruptcy in 1923, years before Steamboat Willie and Snow White. That early collapse is the biographical backdrop against which he offered this line to his daughter and her co-writer in the mid-1950s.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Walt Disney holds up — unusually, for a name this heavily targeted by fake quotes. What goes wrong is the sourcing and the wording, both of which the quote-poster industry strips away.

items.why: Quote Investigator documents that the Saturday Evening Post of 1 December 1956 (page 67) printed the milder form — “A kick in the pants can be the best thing in the world for you” — while the 1957 book printed “a kick in the teeth may be.” QI’s stated suspicion is that Disney approved both, and that he may even have said both across the interview sessions, so neither is a corruption of the other. See Quote Investigator ↗.

It is not from a speech, an essay, a letter or a film. It is reported speech recorded in a book written by someone else — his daughter Diane Disney Miller, “as told to” the Saturday Evening Post writer Pete Martin, who had co-written her 1956 magazine series with her, per Wikipedia ↗.

Most reposts begin at “You may not realize it…” and drop the clause that gives it meaning. Wikiquote ↗ preserves the fuller reading, which opens with Disney saying that all the adversity, troubles and obstacles in his life had strengthened him.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: authentically Disney. Quote Investigator ↗ and Wikiquote ↗ independently land on the same source — The Story of Walt Disney (1957); Quote Investigator pins it to page 89, where it is printed as Disney’s own words.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The line comes out of a very specific piece of mid-1950s publishing. In 1956 Diane Disney Miller, Walt’s eldest daughter, published a series of eight pieces in the Saturday Evening Post called “My Dad, Walt Disney,” co-written with the magazine’s Pete Martin. That material was combined and revised into a book, The Story of Walt Disney, published by Henry Holt the following year — and the “kick in the teeth” sentence appears there, on page 89, inside quotation marks as her father’s own speech.

It reads as a motivational poster now, but in the book it is autobiography rather than advice. Disney’s early career had been a sequence of hard landings — the Laugh-O-Gram company he started in Kansas City went bankrupt in 1923, long before the studio that made him famous. Quote Investigator opens its investigation on exactly that point: the man saying setbacks can be useful had a documented run of them.
context.detailsSummary: The two versions, and where each one came from
detailsBody: Quote Investigator documents two wordings from the same reporting project. The Saturday Evening Post of 1 December 1956 (“The Coming of the Mouse,” page 67) carries the softer “kick in the pants” form; the 1957 book carries “kick in the teeth.” QI’s stated suspicion is that Disney sanctioned both, and that these two publications were the vectors that put the saying into circulation.

The blunter “teeth” version is the one that travelled. QI traces it forward into Alfred Armand Montapert’s compilation Distilled Wisdom (Prentice-Hall, 1964, page 106), then into newspaper filler columns — the Newark Advocate of Newark, Ohio, on 28 June 1966, and the Omaha World Herald on 10 July 1969. Both the 1956 magazine printing and the 1957 book appeared while Disney was alive; he died on 15 December 1966.
context.pull: Not a slogan Disney wrote — a remark his daughter wrote down.
